Set theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Foundations of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 50k Articles: 957
Set theory studies sets, their set elements, and the constructions and sizes possible for them. It supplies a shared vocabulary for mathematics: a function connects two sets, a binary relation specifies which pairs of objects are related, and a probability space starts with a set of possible outcomes. Giving these objects a common language lets a construction from one subject be used in another without repeating its underlying bookkeeping.
A particularly beautiful question is how to compare sizes without first assigning a number. Two sets have the same cardinality when a bijection pairs every member of one with exactly one member of the other. For finite sets, this agrees with ordinary counting. For infinite sets, it produces surprises: n↦2n bijects the natural numbers with the nonnegative even integers, and the Cantor pairing function bijects the Cartesian product N2 with N. A proper subset can have the same cardinality as its containing set.
This does not make all infinite sets equally large. Cantor's diagonal argument shows that all infinite binary sequences cannot be listed by the natural numbers. Cantor's theorem gives the wider principle: the power set of any set has strictly greater cardinality. The contrast between an explicit enumeration and an impossibility argument makes the meaning of infinity much sharper than a picture of something merely continuing forever.
Set formation itself requires care. Russell's paradox shows why not every condition defines a set of all objects satisfying it. Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory instead uses axioms specifying permitted constructions, including set comprehension within a previously given set. The restrictions are useful: they let us form the collections ordinary arguments need while blocking the unrestricted construction that produces the paradox.

ZF without foundation (ZF∗)

Words: 119 Articles: 1
Set theory OurBigBook.com
ZF without foundation consists of the axioms of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of foundation omitted. Ordinal-indexed transfinite recursion still defines the cumulative hierarchy. Its union is the well-founded part and need not include all ambient sets.

Foundation in the cumulative hierarchy without ambient Foundation

Words: 92
ZF without foundation OurBigBook.com
The cumulative hierarchy is a transitive class even without the ambient Axiom of foundation. If a is a nonempty member, choose the least ordinal α with a∩Vα​=∅. It is a successor β+1. An element x of that intersection is a subset of Vβ​, while a has no element in Vβ​, so a∩x=∅. This proves internal Foundation. If the hierarchy also satisfies the other ZF axioms, restricting every quantifier of a finite ZF proof to this definable class translates it into a proof from ZF without foundation. Thus adjoining Foundation preserves consistency relative to the remaining axioms.

Set-theoretic limit

Words: 82 Articles: 1
Set theory OurBigBook.com
For a sequence of sets, the limit superior of sets consists of points belonging to infinitely many members, while the lower limit consists of points belonging to every sufficiently late member. If the two sets coincide, their common value is the set-theoretic limit.

Limit superior of sets (limsupn​En​=⋂N​⋃n≥N​En​)

Words: 45
Set-theoretic limit OurBigBook.com
Membership means that for every index N there is a later n≥N with x∈En​, equivalently membership for infinitely many indices. If ∑n​μ(En​)<∞, countable subadditivity gives μ(limsupEn​)≤∑n≥N​μ(En​)→0. This is the measure form of the first Borel-Cantelli lemma, and requires no independence assumption.

Russell's paradox (R∈R⟺R∈/R)

Words: 146 Articles: 1
Set theory OurBigBook.com
Unrestricted formation of a set R={x:x∈/x} contradicts its own membership condition: substituting R for x gives the displayed equivalence. Thus a predicate cannot always define a set of all objects satisfying it. Restricted set comprehension forms a subset of a previously given set, avoiding this argument. The contradiction does not assert that a set whose elements happen not to contain themselves is impossible; it rules out the universal collection with exactly the specified membership condition.

Barber paradox

Words: 76
Russell's paradox OurBigBook.com
For a binary relation S, no object b can satisfy S(b,p)↔¬S(p,p) for every p. Putting p=b would give s↔¬s for s=S(b,b). The forward direction derives ¬s by a negation introduction subproof assuming s; the reverse direction then gives s, a contradiction. Thus this argument even avoids needing the law of excluded middle. The familiar interpretation reads S(b,p) as “b shaves p”; the logical obstruction is self-application rather than a physical peculiarity of shaving.

Urelement

Words: 185 Articles: 1
Set theory OurBigBook.com
An urelement is an object permitted alongside sets, with no members, distinguished from the empty set by an atom or set predicate. Extensionality is restricted to sets, so distinct atoms need not be equal merely because they have no members. An atom is different from a Quine atom, which is a set with a self-member. In simple typed set theory with atoms, each sort may contain urelements in addition to the objects representing subsets of the preceding sort.

Basic Fraenkel permutation model

Words: 119
Urelement OurBigBook.com
Start with a well-founded universe of sets over an infinite set A of urelements. The full symmetric group of A acts recursively on sets. Retain the objects all of whose descendants have a finite support in a permutation action. This class satisfies set-extensionality, foundation, infinity, pairing, union, separation, replacement and its internal power set axiom. A definable functional image has the finite union of the supports of its domain and parameters as a support; uniqueness makes the image invariant. The family of two-element subsets of A has no choice function: a transposition of two atoms outside the function's finite support fixes their pair and moves either possible choice. For untyped membership with extensionality merely restricted to nonempty objects, atoms are also vacuous subsets; add all atoms to each internal power-set object.

Hereditarily locally small membership model (Bλ​)

Words: 93
Set theory OurBigBook.com
For a strong-limit cardinal λ of countable cofinality, define
Bλ​={x:∀y∈TC({x}) (∣y∣<λ)}.
(1)
Here smallness bounds every individual membership extension; it does not bound the cardinality of the entire transitive closure. The transitive class Bλ​ satisfies all ZF axioms except possibly the Axiom of union: functional images have fewer than λ elements, and the power set of a set of size μ<λ has size 2μ<λ. These facts give Axiom schema of replacement and Axiom of power set; pairs and definable subsets also remain locally small. For λ=ℶω​, the countable set {Vω+n​:n<ω} belongs to Bλ​, but its union Vω+ω​ has size λ and does not. This gives an explicit relative-independence model for the Axiom of union.

New Foundations

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Set theory OurBigBook.com
New Foundations uses ordinary extensionality and comprehension restricted to stratified formulas. Its atom-permitting weakening is New Foundations with urelements.

New Foundations with urelements (NFU)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
New Foundations OurBigBook.com
NFU has a universal domain, a predicate S distinguishing sets from atoms, extensionality restricted to sets, and comprehension for stratified formulas. Atoms have no members. Every stratified predicate has a set extension, including the always-false predicate, so there is a distinguished empty set even when atoms exist. Permitting atoms removes the full-extensionality obstacle in New Foundations.

Type-shifting automorphism (j:Di​⟶Di+1​)

Words: 1k Articles: 3
New Foundations with urelements OurBigBook.com
For an integer-indexed typed model, a type-shifting automorphism is a bijection from each type to the next preserving equality, adjacent-type membership and the set predicates. On type zero define xEy by x∈j(y). Stratified formulas are translated by sending a variable of type i to ji(x). Typed comprehension then gives the untyped comprehension of NFU. Such an automorphism is external; formulas containing it are not included in the typed comprehension scheme.
Rank-shifting automorphism construction of NFU
Words: 1k Articles: 2
Type-shifting automorphism OurBigBook.com
In a model of ZFC, choose an external automorphism j and an ordinal α with j(α)>α. Set Di​=Vji(α)​ for integer i, and declare the sets of type i+1 to be its objects that are subsets of Di​. Ordinary membership between successive types satisfies typed comprehension and set-extensionality. The automorphism shifts all types, yielding NFU by the type-zero collapse. A Skolem hull of integer-indexed increasing ordinal indiscernibles supplies such a j by shifting the indices. The model is externally ill-founded; a transitive well-founded universe cannot have such an automorphism.
Rank-shifting NFU model with explicit set predicate (S(y)⟺j(y)⊆D,xEy⟺S(y)∧x∈j(y))
Words: 1k Articles: 1
Rank-shifting automorphism construction of NFU OurBigBook.com
Let M be a membership structure satisfying extensionality and every pure-membership separation instance, with an external automorphism j and domains Di​=ji(D0​) represented by objects of M. Suppose every M-subset of Di​ is an element of Di+1​. Interpret NFU on the objects of D0​ using the displayed set predicate and membership, with all subset statements evaluated in M. Atoms have no members, and extensionality applied to j(y),j(z)⊆D0​ gives extensionality for sets. A stratified formula becomes an ordinary pure-membership formula by sending each variable of type i to ji(x) and restricting its quantifier to Di​. A set predicate on sort i means containment in Di−1​; adjacent-sort membership is guarded by containment in the lower domain. Separation yields the extension X⊆Di​, the closure hypothesis places it in Di+1​, and j−(i+1)(X)∈D0​ is the required untyped set. This proves every comprehension instance. The guard is essential: an object not contained in a lower domain can still have some ordinary members there, which must not become members of a typed atom. Internal ranks Vji(α)​ with j(α)>α give one instance of these hypotheses; shifted rank objects in an elementary model of an expanded Vω+ω​ give a consistency proof without assuming Con(ZFC).
Rank-indiscernible construction of an NFU model
Words: 807
Rank-shifting NFU model with explicit set predicate OurBigBook.com
NFU has a unary predicate S for sets, atoms have no members, extensionality applies to sets, and comprehension applies to every stratified formula. A stratification assigns integer types to variables so that equality uses equal types and x∈y requires type(y)=type(x)+1. A unary set predicate adds no type difference.
Start with the actual set structure B=(Vω+ω​,∈). This structure satisfies extensionality and every pure-membership separation instance: the subset defined in a set a of rank below ω+ω still has rank below ω+ω. We do not assert that B satisfies replacement or all of ZFC. Expand it by Skolem functions. In it use the sequence of rank objects Vω+n+6​, n<ω. For two such objects d<e in sequence order, we have

with quantifiers in B. The second statement holds because every subset of Vα​ belongs to Vα+1​, and the later rank is at least α+1.

Also require Vω+5​⊆di​ for every i; this fixed rank object is first-order definable in B. Every finite part of these requirements together with Th(B∗) is satisfiable: color finite increasing tuples of the original rank sequence by the truth values of the finitely many formulas mentioned, and use Ramsey's theorem to get a homogeneous subsequence. The rank assertions hold for every increasing tuple there. The compactness theorem gives a model of the full theory. Thus N still satisfies extensionality and all pure-membership separation instances, and
N⊨∀x(x⊆di​⟹x∈di+1​)(i∈Z).

This is a set-sized first-order model; no satisfaction predicate for a proper-class universe is being assumed.
Externally let Di​={x∈N:N⊨x∈di​}. The automorphism bijects Di​ onto Di+1​. Interpret a typed structure with sort i equal to Di​. At sort i+1, declare y a set exactly when N⊨y⊆di​; otherwise it is an atom. Define adjacent-sort membership by
x∈i​y⟺N⊨(y⊆di​ ∧ x∈y).

The guard is necessary: a typed atom might have some ordinary N-members in Di​, and those must not become its typed members. Set-extensionality follows from extensionality in N, because the ordinary members of a typed set all lie in Di​. For any typed formula on sort i, its quantifiers can be restricted to the corresponding dl​, its set predicates replaced by subset assertions, and its memberships replaced by the guarded relation. This is an ordinary pure-membership formula of N with finitely many parameters. Separation gives its extension X⊆di​, and the displayed closure assertion gives X∈di+1​. It is therefore a typed set witnessing comprehension. The automorphism shifts these sorted domains and preserves the set flags and guarded memberships.
Collapse the types onto D0​. Define
S(y)⟺N⊨j(y)⊆d0​,xEy⟺S(y) ∧ N⊨x∈j(y).

Objects not satisfying S have no E-members. If two sets have the same E-members, their images under j are subsets of d0​ with the same ordinary members, so are equal by extensionality of N; injectivity of j gives equality of the original objects.
To verify every stratified comprehension instance, assign a variable v its stratification type t(v) and translate its value a∈D0​ to jt(v)(a)∈Dt(v)​. Equality is preserved. An atomic E(x,y) translates to the guarded adjacent-sort membership because t(y)=t(x)+1; the unary predicate S(y) translates to jt(y)(y)⊆dt(y)−1​. aEb⟺N⊨jt(a)∈X⟺φ(a,p​).

Since j(f)=f, membership of this pair in f under E is equivalent to ⟨x,y⟩N​∈f. Thus f is an internal injection of ω into itself omitting zero, giving a Dedekind-infinite set.
We have built a model of NFU, with infinity if it is included in the formulation, in ordinary ZFC metatheory:
ZFC proves the existence of a model of NFU.​

Words: 65

A formula is stratified if its variables can be assigned integer types so that equality relates variables of the same type and membership x∈y requires type(y)=type(x)+1. Unary set predicates impose no additional difference. Stratification is a syntactic condition; it does not assert that the untyped universe actually has disjoint types. Translating a stratified formula into a typed model permits type-shifting automorphism to recover untyped comprehension.

An equivalence relation says which set elements should count as the same for a particular purpose. In modular arithmetic, for example, distinct integers with the same remainder are equivalent. The relation gathers interchangeable set elements into equivalence classes; the quotient set then treats each whole equivalence class as one object.
Formally, an equivalence relation on a set X is a binary relation R⊆X×X, written x∼y, satisfying three conditions for all x,y,z∈X:
  • Reflexivity: x∼x.
  • Symmetric relation: x∼y implies y∼x.
  • Transitivity: x∼y and y∼z imply x∼z.
These conditions make the equivalence classes a partition of a set: each set element belongs to exactly one class. [ref]
For a worked example, take the finite set X={0,1,…,8} and restrict integer congruence modulo three to X:
x∼y⟺x≡y(mod3)⟺3∣(x−y).
(13)
Reflexivity follows because x−x=0. The symmetric relation property follows by changing the sign of a difference, and transitivity follows by adding x−y and y−z: divisibility by three is preserved in both steps. Thus 0∼3 and 3∼6 force 0∼6. The three equivalence classes are {0,3,6}, {1,4,7} and {2,5,8}. Their members alternate along the number line; membership in an equivalence class need not mean being close together.
The transitivity requirement rules out a tempting alternative. On {0,1,2}, define nearness by the absolute value condition ∣x−y∣≤1. This binary relation is reflexive and symmetric, but 0 is near 1 and 1 is near 2 while 0 is not near 2. Its neighborhoods {0,1}, {0,1,2} and {1,2} overlap without being equal. They are not equivalence classes or a partition of a set.

It has cardinality three. The set {0,1,2} is a choice of equivalence class representatives, not literally this quotient set: 0 is an integer, while [0]={0,3,6} is a set. The function sending each chosen equivalence class representative to its equivalence class is a bijection between these two different sets.
A quotient set alone specifies no arithmetic. To obtain the familiar modular arithmetic example with addition, use integer congruence on the whole set of integers. Its quotient set is Z/3Z={[0]3​,[1]3​,[2]3​}, where [a]3​={a+3k:k∈Z} is an infinite residue class. Define addition by
[a]3​+[b]3​=[a+b]3​.
(19)
The answer must be independent of the equivalence class representatives. If a′=a+3k and b′=b+3ℓ, then a′+b′=a+b+3(k+ℓ), so both sums have the same residue class. This is what it means for the group operation to be well-defined. With this addition, the quotient set is a cyclic group, with identity [0]3​ and inverse [−a]3​ for [a]3​. [ref]
For example, [2]3​+[2]3​=[4]3​=[1]3​. Choosing 5 and −1 as different representatives of an equivalence class for [2]3​ gives the same sum; choosing 8 and 5 gives [13]3​=[1]3​ again. These calculations use residue classes of all integers. Raw addition on the finite X={0,…,8} does not stay in X: 8+8=16∈/X. The formula for addition on Z/3Z therefore cannot be applied as a raw inherited operation on that finite example.

q−1({[x]})=[x].

Here the left side is the preimage of a singleton subset of the quotient set; its members are the original set elements in the class [x]. In the diagram, the three arrows arriving at [1] start at 1, 4 and 7.

Zorn's lemma

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Set theory OurBigBook.com
Let (P,≤) be a nonempty partially ordered set. If every chain in a partial order C⊆P has an upper bound in P, then P has a maximal element. The hypothesis means
∀C⊆P that is a chain,∃u∈P∀c∈C, c≤u.
(21)
The upper bound may depend on C and need not belong to C. A least upper bound is not required. The conclusion asserts that some m∈P satisfies m≤x⟹x=m; it does not assert a greatest element, which would satisfy x≤m for every x∈P.[ref]
Here a chain in a partial order may be the empty set. Every member of P is an upper bound of the empty chain in a partial order, so including it in the hypothesis already forces P to be nonempty. If “chain” means only nonempty chains in a partial order, the separate nonempty-P assumption is essential: the empty poset otherwise satisfies the hypothesis vacuously and has no maximal element. These are two equivalent conventions for the theorem.
The strength of Zorn's lemma is that compatible partial constructions can have a completed, unextendible member without an explicit procedure for finding it. The next examples separate the upper bound calculation from the reason a maximal element has the desired property. All chains in a partial order must be covered, including uncountable ones, rather than just increasing sequences. The condition is sufficient, not necessary: a poset can have a maximal element and still have an unbounded chain in a partial order elsewhere.

Zorn's lemma in a finite poset

Words: 202
Zorn's lemma OurBigBook.com
Consider the following finite set of subsets, ordered by subset containment:
P={∅,{a},{b},{c},{a,b},{b,c}}.
(22)
Every nonempty chain in a partial order has a greatest element within that chain in a partial order, hence an upper bound in P. For the empty chain in a partial order, choose ∅∈P. Thus the hypothesis of Zorn's lemma holds. The two maximal elements are {a,b} and {b,c}: neither is a proper subset of another member of P. There is no greatest element, because it would have to contain both, and no member of P contains {a,b,c}.
For the chain in a partial order C={∅,{b}}, the member {b} is already an upper bound, although it is not a maximal element of P. Both orange members are also upper bounds for C. A chain in a partial order need not have a unique upper bound, and the upper bound used to check the hypothesis need not be the eventual maximal element.
The restriction to chains in a partial order matters. The subset {{a},{c}}⊆P has no upper bound in P, but its two members are incomparable, so it is not a chain in a partial order. Requiring every subset of P to have an upper bound would be much stronger: taking that subset to be P itself would force a greatest element.

Vector space bases from Zorn's lemma (∃B⊆V: B is a basis of V)

Words: 267
Zorn's lemma OurBigBook.com
Every vector space V over a field F has a basis, assuming the axiom of choice. More generally, any linearly independent subset A⊆V extends to a basis. This is an algebraic Hamel basis: each representation uses a finite linear combination, even when the basis is infinite.[ref]
Use the poset of linearly independent subsets containing A:
PA​={S⊆V:A⊆S, S is linearly independent over F},S≤T⟺S⊆T.
(23)
It is a set, being a subset of the power set of V, and is nonempty because A∈PA​.
A short proof outline supplies both essential steps:
  • For a nonempty chain in a partial order C⊆PA​, put U=⋃S∈C​S. Any finite linear relation in U lies in one member of C: among finitely many containing members, one contains the rest. Its linear independence makes every coefficient zero. Thus U∈PA​ is an upper bound. For the empty chain in a partial order, use A; its empty union need not contain A.
  • Zorn's lemma gives a maximal element B. If a vector v lies outside its linear span, then B∪{v} is linearly independent: a linear relation with nonzero coefficient on v would express v in that linear span. This contradicts maximality, so B is a spanning set and hence a basis.[ref]
Taking A=∅ proves existence, including V={0}, whose basis is the empty set. The chain in a partial order need not be indexed by the natural numbers: only the finitely many members needed for a particular linear relation are compared. An arbitrary union of linearly independent sets can fail: {v} and {2v} for a nonzero vector over the real numbers are each linearly independent, but their union is linearly dependent. The nesting of a chain in a partial order is what prevents this failure.

Finite greedy basis extension and choice

Words: 251
Zorn's lemma OurBigBook.com
For an explicit basis extension in R2, start with A={u}, where u=(1,1). Its linear span is the line y=x. Adding w=(1,−1) preserves linear independence, because w is outside that line, and gives a basis. Every vector has the finite linear combination
(x,y)=2x+y​u+2x−y​w.
(24)
The vector 2u=(2,2) cannot be added while preserving linear independence: it is already in the linear span. Many choices outside the line work, so maximality does not select a unique basis.
For a finite-dimensional vector space with a supplied finite spanning set, a greedy algorithm scans the list, retaining each vector precisely when it is outside the linear span of those already retained. Starting with a linearly independent A, the same scan adjoins only the needed vectors. Retained vectors remain linearly independent, and every skipped vector is in the final linear span, so the result is a basis containing A. Finite reasoning needs no axiom of choice.
For an arbitrary vector space, this finite stopping argument is unavailable. Accepting Zorn's lemma asserts existence of a maximal element once every chain in a partial order has an upper bound; it supplies no general computational recipe. Over ZF, Zorn's lemma, the axiom of choice and the well-ordering theorem are equivalent. Particular infinite vector spaces can still have explicit bases, such as 1,x,x2,… for the vector space of univariate polynomials over a specified field; infinity alone does not force a nonconstructive argument.[ref]

Proof outline of Zorn's lemma

Words: 122
Zorn's lemma OurBigBook.com
Assume the axiom of choice and suppose a poset satisfying the hypothesis has no maximal element. Fix a choice function on its nonempty subsets. By transfinite recursion, choose at each ordinal stage an upper bound of the chain in a partial order already constructed, then choose a strictly larger member. Both choices are available, including the initial empty stage. This produces distinct members throughout the Hartogs ordinal of P, contradicting the Hartogs theorem. Thus a maximal element exists. Conversely, apply Zorn's lemma to partial choice functions on a family of nonempty sets, ordered by extension. A chain in a partial order has the compatible union as an upper bound, and a maximal element must be defined on the whole family, since one missing value could be adjoined.
Zorn's lemma was introduced in 1935 to shorten algebra proofs using choice or the well-ordering theorem.[ref]

Image and preimage of a function

Words: 766 Articles: 3
Set theory OurBigBook.com
The image of a function asks which outputs a chosen set of inputs reaches. A preimage asks which inputs reach a chosen set of outputs. Both constructions apply to every function, including one that loses information by sending several inputs to the same output. Their difference is useful whenever a transformation must be followed forward or a condition on its result must be traced back.
Consider the function f:A→B with
A={a,b,c,d},B={0,1,2,3},f(a)=f(b)=0,f(c)=1,f(d)=2.
(32)
Every input has exactly one output, but zero has two inputs and three has none. The full image of a function is f(A)={0,1,2}, a proper subset of the codomain B. Selecting inputs {a,c} gives image {0,1}. Selecting outputs {0,2} instead gives preimage {a,b,d}.
The function is not injective, because f(a)=f(b), and is not surjective onto B, because three is absent from its image. Restricting only the codomain to {0,1,2} makes the same rule surjective; it remains noninjective. This separates the output set actually reached from the target set specified in the definition. The definitions of images of a function and preimages, including the distinction from an inverse function, are given in Richard Hammack, Book of Proof, §12.6: Image and Preimage.

Image of a function (f(X))

Words: 208

For a function f:X→Y and a subset E⊆X, its image is
f(E)={f(x):x∈E}={y∈Y: there exists x∈E with f(x)=y}.
(33)
The full image of a function is f(X). The set notation ignores repeated outputs: in the finite example above, f({a,b})={0}, rather than a list containing zero twice. A function collision can therefore reduce the cardinality of an image.
Images of a function preserve unions:
f(E∪F)=f(E)∪f(F).
(34)
An output reached from the union is reached from at least one of its two input sets. For intersections, however, only
f(E∩F)⊆f(E)∩f(F)
(35)
holds in general. In the finite example, take E={a} and F={b}. Their intersection is the empty set, so f(E∩F)=∅. But f(E)=f(F)={0}, giving f(E)∩f(F)={0}. Distinct witnesses in the two input sets can produce the same output.
For an injective function, an output shared by f(E) and f(F) must come from the same input. That input lies in E∩F, so equality holds. Conversely, preserving intersections for every pair of input subsets forces injectivity: two distinct inputs with the same output would give the singleton counterexample above. The image and preimage laws are stated in Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis I, Propositions 0.3.15–0.3.16; the finite example makes the missing reverse inclusion visible.

Words: 340 Articles: 1

For a function f:X→Y and a subset U⊆Y, its preimage is
f−1(U)={x∈X:f(x)∈U}.
(36)
It is a subset of the original domain of a function. The notation does not require an inverse function: the preimage of a singleton set can have no members, one member, or many members. In the finite example, f−1({0})={a,b}, f−1({1})={c} and f−1({3})=∅. The preimage of a singleton set is also its fiber of a function.
For subsets U,V⊆Y, preimages preserve both unions and intersections:
f−1(U∪V)=f−1(U)∪f−1(V),f−1(U∩V)=f−1(U)∩f−1(V).
(37)
For the intersection, the same input x belongs precisely when its single output f(x) belongs to both U and V. There is no opportunity to choose different witnesses, which is what made the image counterexample fail. The identities also hold for arbitrary families of output subsets.
In the finite example, choose U={0,1} and V={0,2}. Then
f−1(U)={a,b,c},f−1(V)={a,b,d},f−1(U∩V)=f−1({0})={a,b}.
(38)
The intersection of the two preimages is exactly the same set {a,b}. Complements are preserved with respect to the appropriate source and target sets:
f−1(Y∖U)=X∖f−1(U).
(39)
For example, the unused output three contributes no extra input: with U={0,2}, both sides of the complement identity are {c}. See Lebl, Proposition 0.3.15: preimages of unions, intersections and complements.
This makes preimages useful for transporting conditions. The solution set of g(x)=0 is g−1({0}), and a zero set is a preimage of zero. Requiring two output conditions takes the intersection of their preimages. In topology, a continuous function pulls every open set back to an open set; a measurable function pulls the specified measurable sets in its codomain back to measurable sets in its domain of a function. These definitions use preimages because their set operations remain consistent even when the function is noninjective.

For proper filters on positive integers, define A∈F+G when {x:A−x∈G}∈F. This is again a proper filter. The inner truth-set map preserves the whole set, the empty set, inclusions and finite intersections; applying the outer filter gives all filter axioms. The order of the two filter quantifiers is part of the definition and is not silently interchangeable.

Filter quantifier (∀F​xp(x))

Words: 133 Articles: 2
Filter (set theory) OurBigBook.com
For a proper filter on a set, write ∀F​xp(x) when the truth set {x:p(x)} belongs to the filter. This quantifier preserves finite conjunctions. For an ultrafilter it also preserves finite disjunctions and obeys classical negation; a general proper filter need not have those latter properties.

Boolean failure of the cofinite-filter quantifier

Words: 54
Filter quantifier OurBigBook.com
The even and odd integers are both absent from the cofinite filter, but their union is present. Thus its filter quantifier need not turn a disjunction into the disjunction of quantified assertions, and failure of a quantified assertion need not imply truth of its quantified negation. An ultrafilter restores both laws by deciding each set against its complement.

Conjunction law for filter quantifiers (∀F​(p∧q)⟺(∀F​p)∧(∀F​q))

Words: 37
Filter quantifier OurBigBook.com
The filter quantifier satisfies ∀F​(p∧q) if and only if both ∀F​p and ∀F​q. Finite-intersection closure gives one direction and upward closure gives the other. Properness ensures contradictory truth sets cannot both be filter members.

Free filter

Words: 119 Articles: 1
Filter (set theory) OurBigBook.com
A free filter on a set I has empty intersection of all its members. This is equivalent to containing every cofinite subset of I: for each i some filter member omits i, so upward closure gives I∖{i}, and finite intersections give every cofinite set. A proper free filter on an infinite set contains no finite set.

Membership in a free filter is detected by its ultrafilter extensions

Words: 64
Free filter OurBigBook.com
For a free filter F, a subset S belongs to F if and only if every ultrafilter extending F contains S. If S∈/F, every A∈F meets I∖S in an infinite set; otherwise a cofinite restriction of A would be contained in S. Adjoining I∖S therefore generates a proper free filter. The ultrafilter lemma extends it to a nonprincipal ultrafilter witnessing failure of membership.

Kappa-complete filter (κ-complete)

Words: 44 Articles: 1
Filter (set theory) OurBigBook.com
A filter is κ-complete when the intersection of every family of fewer than κ members again belongs to the filter.

Cobounded filter on a regular cardinal

Words: 23
Kappa-complete filter OurBigBook.com
The cobounded filter on a regular cardinal κ consists of sets whose complements have cardinality below κ. Regularity makes it κ-complete.

Cofinite filter

Words: 65 Articles: 1
Filter (set theory) OurBigBook.com
The cofinite filter on an infinite set consists of all subsets whose complements are finite.

Cofinite set

Words: 50
Cofinite filter OurBigBook.com
A subset E of a set X is cofinite in X when its complement X∖E is a finite set. For infinite X, the cofinite subsets form the cofinite filter. A nonprincipal ultrafilter on N contains every cofinite subset: it contains no singleton, hence no finite set, and decides between each set and its complement.

Ultrafilter lemma

Words: 142 Articles: 1
Filter (set theory) OurBigBook.com
Every proper filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter. Order its proper filter extensions by inclusion, use Zorn lemma to obtain a maximal extension, and observe that maximality forces it to contain exactly one of every set and its complement.

Ultrafilter selection from a partition-rich family

Words: 106
Ultrafilter lemma OurBigBook.com
Let S be a nonempty set and P⊆P(S) be upward closed. An ultrafilter all of whose members lie in P exists exactly when every finite set partition of S has a cell in P. For sufficiency, the complements of sets outside P have the finite intersection property: a finite cover by such sets could be disjointified into a partition with no cell in P. The ultrafilter lemma extends the generated proper filter. Necessity follows because an ultrafilter selects exactly one cell of every finite partition. This criterion requires partition richness of the whole ground set; it does not assert that the complement family is closed under unions.

Ultrafilter

Words: 1k Articles: 25
Filter (set theory) OurBigBook.com
An ultrafilter on a set X is a proper filter on a set that contains exactly one of A and X∖A for every A⊆X.

Fine ultrafilter ({x:α∈x}∈U)

Words: 84 Articles: 1
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
An ultrafilter on Pκ​(λ) is fine when it contains the set of small subsets containing α, for each α<λ. Fineness makes every coordinate of λ represented in the corresponding ultrapower, though no one small subset is required to contain every coordinate.
Normal ultrafilter on small subsets
Words: 42
Fine ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
An ultrafilter U on Pκ​(λ) is normal when each function with f(x)∈x on a U-large set is constant on a U-large subset. This is the small-subset version of normality; together with fineness and kappa-completeness it gives the measure characterization of a supercompact cardinal.

Normal ultrafilter on a cardinal (Δα<κ​Xα​∈U)

Words: 53
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
A uniform kappa-complete ultrafilter U on an uncountable cardinal κ is normal if every regressive function on a U-large set is constant on a U-large subset. Equivalently it is closed under diagonal intersections Δα<κ​Xα​={β<κ:(∀α<β) β∈Xα​}. Normality supplies homogeneous sets for pair-colourings by combining the chosen large tail at each earlier coordinate.

Ultrafilter with arithmetic-progression-rich members (U⊆AP)

Words: 46
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
An ultrafilter on the positive integers with every member containing finite arithmetic progressions of arbitrarily large length. The Van der Waerden theorem and ultrafilter selection from a partition-rich family give existence. Such an ultrafilter must contain the complement of every set with bounded arithmetic-progression length, and it is a nonprincipal ultrafilter. No corresponding ultrafilter can have an infinite arithmetic progression in every member, by the dyadic block obstruction to infinite arithmetic progressions.

Ultrafilter with finite-sums members

Words: 71
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
An ultrafilter with finite-sums members is an ultrafilter on the positive integers all of whose members are IP sets. Such an ultrafilter exists by extending the IP-star filter using the ultrafilter lemma. If a member were not IP, its complement would be an IP-star set and hence another member, contradicting properness. Conversely, every such ultrafilter contains the entire IP-star filter, since it cannot contain the non-IP complement of an IP-star set. This characterization does not assert that the ultrafilter is idempotent.

Number of ultrafilters on an infinite set (∣Ult(X)∣=22∣X∣)

Words: 49
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
The finite-trace independent family construction gives 2∣X∣ independent subsets of an infinite X. Each binary assignment generates a proper filter and, in ZFC, has an ultrafilter extension. Different assignments force incompatible membership decisions, giving 22∣X∣ distinct ultrafilters. The matching upper bound follows because every ultrafilter is a subset of P(X).

Pushforward ultrafilter (g∗​U={B⊆Y:g−1[B]∈U})

Words: 52
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
For an ultrafilter U on X and a function g:X→Y, define g∗​U={B⊆Y:g−1[B]∈U}. This is an ultrafilter and inherits countable completeness from a countably complete ultrafilter. It is nonprincipal exactly when no single fibre of g belongs to U. Restricting U to a member of U before pushing forward preserves these properties.

Fubini product of ultrafilters (U⊗V)

Words: 85
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
For ultrafilters U on I and V on J, put
A∈U⊗V⟺{i∈I:{j∈J:(i,j)∈A}∈V}∈U.
(41)
This is an ultrafilter on I×J: upward closure and finite intersection follow at both levels, and the ultrafilter dichotomy follows by complementing at both levels. Iterating gives ordered finite products. Projection onto a subsequence of coordinates pushes this product to the product on that subsequence, since omitted coordinates are absent from the tested first-order formula. The order of coordinates matters; these products need not be symmetric.

Ultrafilter functor (U)

Words: 77 Articles: 1
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
The ultrafilter functor sends a set A to its set U(A) of ultrafilters. A function f:A→B acts by pushforward,
f∗​U={C⊆B:f−1(C)∈U}.
(42)
It preserves finite coproducts: an ultrafilter on A⊔B contains exactly one summand and is uniquely induced by an ultrafilter on that summand.
Terminal finite-coproduct-preserving set endofunctor
Words: 30
Ultrafilter functor OurBigBook.com
The ultrafilter functor is terminal among endofunctors of Set that preserve finite coproducts. For such an endofunctor F and x∈F(A), the unique natural map sends x to
{B⊆A:x∈im(F(B)→F(A))}.
(43)

Principal ultrafilter

Words: 26
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
The principal ultrafilter at x∈X is {A⊆X:x∈A}. An ultraproduct by a principal ultrafilter is isomorphic to the factor indexed by x.

Nonprincipal ultrafilter

Words: 55 Articles: 1
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
A nonprincipal ultrafilter contains no finite set. On an infinite set it contains the cofinite filter.
Small set is absent from a complete nonprincipal ultrafilter
Words: 40
Nonprincipal ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
If U is a nonprincipal κ-complete ultrafilter on X and A⊆X has cardinality below κ, then A∈/U. Indeed, every X∖{a} belongs to U, so κ-completeness puts their intersection X∖A in U.

Countably complete ultrafilter

Words: 37
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
An ultrafilter is countably complete when the intersection of every countable family of its members again belongs to it. Equivalently, whenever the underlying set is partitioned into countably many pieces, exactly one piece belongs to the ultrafilter.

Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers (βN)

Words: 457 Articles: 8
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
The Stone-Cech compactification βN can be identified with the space of ultrafilters on N. Its basic clopen sets are Aˉ={U:A∈U}.
This is the natural-number-space case of Stone-Čech compactification.
No nontrivial convergent sequences in the Stone-Čech compactification
Words: 51
Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers OurBigBook.com
Every convergent sequence in the Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers is eventually constant. If distinct ultrafilters Un​ converged, isolate each from the other sequence terms using convergence and finitely many separating clopen sets. Finite disjointification gives disjoint Bn​∈Un​. The union of the even-indexed Bn​ then belongs exactly to the even-indexed ultrafilters, contradicting convergence of membership in a clopen set.
Compact Hausdorff topology on ultrafilters
Words: 58
Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers OurBigBook.com
For A⊆N, the basic set A={U:A∈U} in the Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers is a clopen set, since its complement is N∖A​. Distinct ultrafilters are separated by complementary basic sets. A basic cover with no finite subcover would give complements with the finite intersection property, whose generated filter on a set extends to an ultrafilter missing the entire cover. Thus the space is a compact Hausdorff space.
Addition on the Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers (+ on βN)
Words: 314 Articles: 5
Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers OurBigBook.com
For ultrafilters U,V∈βN, define U+V by
A∈U+V⟺{x:{y:x+y∈A}∈V}∈U.
(44)
This operation is associative, and each right translation U↦U+V is continuous, so βN is a compact Hausdorff left-topological semigroup.
Idempotent ultrafilter (U+U=U)
Words: 243 Articles: 3
Addition on the Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers OurBigBook.com
An additive idempotent ultrafilter satisfies U+U=U. On positive integers it is necessarily nonprincipal, since a principal ultrafilter at n adds to itself to give the principal ultrafilter at 2n. The idempotent-ultrafilter star-set lemma converts this algebraic property into a recursive construction of finite sums. If zero is included, the trivial principal idempotent at zero must be excluded for that increasing-sequence application.
Tail finite-sums semigroup (K=⋂r​FS(xr​,xr+1​,…)​)
Words: 73
Idempotent ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
For a sequence of positive integers, the nested closures of its tail finite-sums sets have nonempty compact intersection in the Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers. This intersection is a subsemigroup. For a sum s from one tail, all sums supported beyond a chosen finite representation of s lie in that tail translated by −s. The ultrafilter addition formula then establishes closure under addition. The Ellis–Numakura lemma supplies an idempotent ultrafilter containing every tail finite-sums set and hence any set containing the full finite-sums set.
Zero-residue constraint for idempotent ultrafilters (p selects 0(modq))
Words: 51
Idempotent ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
An ultrafilter on the positive integers selects exactly one residue class modulo a fixed positive integer q. Under addition on the Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers, selected residues add. An idempotent ultrafilter must therefore select a residue r with 2r=r in the finite cyclic group, hence r=0. In particular, the multiples of every fixed positive integer belong to every additive idempotent ultrafilter.
Idempotent-ultrafilter star-set lemma (A∗={n∈A:A−n∈U})
Words: 57
Idempotent ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
For A∈U and an idempotent ultrafilter, put A∗={n∈A:A−n∈U}. Then A∗∈U, and A∗−n∈U for every n∈A∗. For the second assertion, apply idempotence to A−n and intersect its resulting good-translation set with A−n. This allows each new finite-sums generator to be chosen from finitely many translation constraints, proving the Idempotent-ultrafilter proof of Hindman's theorem.
Idempotent ultrafilter on the natural numbers
Words: 27
Addition on the Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers OurBigBook.com
An ultrafilter U∈βN is idempotent when U+U=U. The Ellis–Numakura lemma guarantees such an ultrafilter and supplies the main algebraic input to the Idempotent-ultrafilter proof of Hindman's theorem.

Ultralimit

Words: 102 Articles: 1
Ultrafilter OurBigBook.com
A point x is the limit of a map f:I→X along an ultrafilter U on I when f−1(V)∈U for every neighbourhood V of x. Every ultrafilter on a compact space has a limit, and that limit is unique in a Hausdorff space.
Ultrafilter characterization of compact Hausdorff spaces (∀U ∃!x:U→x)
Words: 60
Ultralimit OurBigBook.com
A topological space is both a compact space and a Hausdorff space exactly when every ultrafilter on its underlying set converges to exactly one point. Existence of all ultrafilter limits characterizes compactness. If a space is not Hausdorff, two distinct points have neighbourhood systems whose combined finite intersections are nonempty; the ultrafilter lemma extends these to an ultrafilter converging to both points. Conversely, disjoint neighbourhoods prevent such a common limit.
